value.overview: The Dusky Nightjar (Antrostomus saturatus), also called the Dusky Whip-poor-will, is a small, secretive nightjar of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is most active after dusk and before dawn, when it hunts flying insects from low perches. Its mottled brown, gray, buff, and black plumage provides excellent camouflage among leaf litter, grass, and forest-edge vegetation. The species is usually detected by its distinctive trilled song rather than by sight.
value.classification: The Dusky Nightjar belongs to the nightjar family Caprimulgidae and the order Caprimulgiformes. It is closely related to other New World whip-poor-wills and nightjars in the genus Antrostomus.
value.identification: This medium-sized nightjar has dark brown to gray-brown upperparts marked with buff and black, creating a strongly mottled appearance. The underparts are warm buff or cinnamon with dark barring. It has a blackish bill, grayish legs, and cryptic plumage suited to roosting on the ground or among vegetation. Adult males may show white markings on the throat and tail; females are generally duller and have reduced or absent white tail markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The Dusky Nightjar has a restricted Central American range in the highlands of Costa Rica and Panama. In Costa Rica, it is a locally common resident of the Central Volcanic Cordillera and Talamanca Cordillera, including the Dota region, generally above 2,000 meters. It also occurs in the Tilarán Cordillera above about 1,500 meters. It favors humid montane forest edges, canopy openings, páramo transitions, high-elevation pastures with scattered trees, clearings, grass, and fern-covered slopes rather than dense forest interiors.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Dusky Nightjar is considered a resident and is generally sedentary. Reliable sources do not indicate regular long-distance migration; substantial seasonal movements are not well documented.
value.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly from February or March through April, although males may begin singing actively as early as December. The species does not build a substantial nest. A single white egg is laid directly on leaf litter or bare ground, often beneath grass or among ferns at a forest edge or in a clearing. The known nesting sites are commonly on sloping ground, where surrounding vegetation helps conceal the egg and incubating adult.
value.dietFeeding: The Dusky Nightjar is an aerial insectivore. It feeds primarily after dark by launching from a low or moderately elevated perch and catching flying insects in short sallies. Beetles and moths appear to be important prey, although other night-flying insects are probably taken as well. It usually forages in forest openings, along edges, and above grassy clearings, and it is less often seen feeding directly from the ground.
value.behavior: This nightjar is nocturnal, solitary, and highly camouflaged. During daylight it rests quietly on the ground or on a low perch, relying on its mottled plumage to remain unnoticed. Males sing from perches, especially during the breeding season and on moonlit nights. The song is a distinctive repeated, trilled double note, while the flight call is a rough or scratchy sound. Individuals are considered notably sedentary within suitable mountain habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although it is restricted in range and not extensively studied.
